prompt.context: Our client is a meat processing company. They buy livestock, process and then sell to major retail supermarket chains. In the early 1990s, the industry went through consolidation and now there are only 5 big players in the market. During this time our client bought about 8 regional/local players in the market who were not doing well and had old assets that had depreciated.
prompt.question: The CEO has called McKinsey because their profitability is declining and they want to understand what they can do. What are the key areas you would look into?

clarifying_info.q: Are revenues declining, costs increasing, or both?
clarifying_info.a: Processing costs are high for the client.

clarifying_info.q: How does our cost structure compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Competitive benchmarking data will be provided comparing the client's Birds division to King Chicken.

clarifying_info.q: Do all plants process the same type of bird?
clarifying_info.a: One of the 10 plants processes turkey instead of chicken; King Chicken only processes chicken. It costs twice as much to process a turkey as a chicken.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking: Client vs. King Chicken
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of average quantity of birds processed per year per plant and average processing cost per bird between the client and King Chicken.

exhibits.title: Client Plant Breakdown: Turkey vs. Chicken
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the client's 10 plants showing quantity of birds processed per year per plant and number of plants for turkey and chicken respectively.

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; investigate whether revenue is declining or costs are increasing

Revenue side: examine price changes and volume changes; assess market growth, competitor pricing/share, and customer trends (e.g., shift to healthier foods or vegetarianism); assess supermarket bargaining power on shelf space and pricing
Cost side - Fixed: plant/facility rent, processing equipment, insurance, SG&A
Cost side - Variable (COGS): direct materials (livestock, chemicals), direct labor, production costs; transportation (each facility is self-contained)
Benchmark costs against competitors to isolate the specific cost driver

questions.prompt: Given the benchmarking data (Exhibit 1), what do you observe and what might explain the cost difference?
questions.guidance: Client processes 300,000 birds/plant at $30/bird vs. King Chicken's 500,000 birds/plant at $20/bird. Candidate should identify economies of scale and capacity utilization as primary drivers, and consider equipment/technology differences, product mix differences (premium vs. commodity), and the possibility that some plants skew the average upward.

questions.prompt: One of the 10 plants processes turkey instead of chicken, and it costs twice as much to process a turkey as a chicken (Exhibit 2). What are the actual per-bird processing costs for chicken and turkey at the client?
questions.guidance: Set up an equation using weighted total cost across all plants equal to the known average. Let cost per chicken = $X, cost per turkey = $2X. Solve for X.

math.setup: Let processing cost per chicken = $X; processing cost per turkey = $2X. Total cost across all plants must equal average cost per bird times total birds: 300,000 birds/plant * $30/bird * 10 plants = $90,000,000 total cost. Alternatively, sum by plant type: (600,000 * $2X * 1) + (266,000 * $X * 9) = 300,000 * $30 * 10
math.answer: Cost per chicken = $25; Cost per turkey = $50

questions.prompt: The chicken processing cost is $25 vs. King Chicken's $20. Why might this gap exist and what should the client do?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the $5 gap (~25% higher) exposes the client competitively given the commodity nature of meat. If the product is undifferentiated, margin pressure is severe. If premium, the price premium must justify the cost gap -- at two pounds of meat per bird, consumers pay ~$2.50 extra per pound, which is significant. Candidate should recommend cost reduction strategies.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions could the client take to reduce both fixed and variable processing costs?

categories.name: Consolidation & Capacity
ideas: Consolidate underutilized plants to spread fixed costs over higher volume
Sell or lease unused plant capacity to third parties
Expand to new markets to increase capacity utilization

categories.name: Synergies from Acquisitions
ideas: Consolidate purchasing across all facilities for better supplier pricing
Share best practices and operational standards across plants
Standardize equipment and processes across acquired facilities

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Improve labor productivity through training or process redesign
Source cheaper labor without sacrificing quality
Reduce headcount through automation where feasible

categories.name: Materials & Suppliers
ideas: Find better or cheaper livestock suppliers
Consolidate supplier relationships to negotiate volume discounts

categories.name: Equipment & Technology
ideas: Invest in newer, more efficient processing equipment
Lease rather than buy equipment to reduce capital expenditure
Adopt advanced processing technology to reduce per-unit cost

categories.name: Product Mix
ideas: Stop processing turkey to eliminate the high-cost plant and lower blended average cost
Evaluate whether premium positioning truly justifies the cost premium

recommendation: The client's profitability decline is primarily driven by high processing costs -- $25/bird for chicken vs. competitor benchmark of $20/bird, and $50/bird for turkey

Priority actions: consolidate plants to achieve economies of scale, capture synergies from past acquisitions (centralized purchasing, shared best practices), and evaluate exiting the turkey processing business to improve blended cost metrics
risks: Consolidation may face labor and community opposition and require significant upfront capital
Exiting turkey may reduce revenue diversification
Cost reduction efforts must not compromise product quality if client is pursuing a premium positioning
next_steps: Conduct plant-by-plant profitability analysis to identify the worst-performing facilities and consolidation candidates
Quantify synergy potential from centralizing purchasing and sharing best practices across the 10 plants
Model the financial impact of exiting turkey processing
Assess whether $5/bird cost gap vs. King Chicken can be closed to competitive parity
